title: This C struct wastes 4 bytes and it's the field order
description:
Two C structs with the exact same three fields can have different sizes, purely because of declaration order. This Short shows why sizeof surprises you: the compiler inserts invisible padding bytes so each field lands on an aligned address. Reorder wide members first and the struct shrinks for free. Full walkthrough, plus unions and bit-fields, in the lesson.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-2/04-structs-unions-advanced/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Two structs. Same three fields, same data. One is twelve bytes, the other is eight. You didn't add anything. So where did those extra four bytes come from?
Here they are. Bad holds a char, then an int, then a char. Good puts the int first, then both chars. Only the order changed.
Run it. Bad is twelve bytes, Good is eight. The CPU wants that int on a four-byte boundary, so the compiler quietly inserts padding after the first char to line it up.

display.output:
sizeof(struct Bad)  = 12
sizeof(struct Good) = 8
Bad:  a@0 b@4 c@8
Good: b@0 a@4 c@5

beats.narration: So the fix is free. Declare your wide members first, doubles and pointers, then the narrow ones. Same fields, less memory, no tricks.
There's more in the full lesson, including unions and bit-fields.
